prompt: Human: What can you tell me about the philosophy of John Locke
response:
The Lockeistas believe that Locke's republicanism and skepticism are the bedrock of their brand of feminism.  They see him as the first truly feminist thinker, and they trace his ideas through to modern feminism.  To them, Locke is the touchstone by which they measure other feminist thinkers, as different thinkers either "fit" or "don't fit" with Locke's political and philosophical principles.

Locke's political philosophy can be best understood in the context of his doctrine of rights.  In his Treatise on Government, Locke develops a version of the social contract, in which he argues that individuals give up some of their natural rights in order to be governed by a state, and in return the state owes those same rights to the individuals.  The state can only do so well by working closely with both the rulers and the subjects, and this requires that it respect and protect the individual's rights.  Locke's emphasis on the 'necessity of the consent of the governed' is meant to mean that the people will give their consent up to a state that is actually inimical to their interests, and that only through their consciences will they revolt.  

Locke also sees himself as writing about the common good, and develops a version of the utilitarianism that underlies his political philosophy.  Utilitarianism is the view that the greatest good can be obtained with the least pain and suffering.  If we consider a series of events in which a person is given the chance to save two children from a burning building versus one who will be killed in the fire, we can consider each event a good in and of itself.  It is only necessary to weigh the numbers and decide which is better.  In this way we are justified in treating all humans with the same disregard that we treat the two children who are saved in the fire.  To act as a utilitarian means acting in the best possible interest of the majority.  This is what our state and our social contract is about, acting as a good for the common good.  

One of Locke's most controversial ideas is his skepticism.  Before the era of empirical science, there were a great many people who believed in magic and the supernatural.  If anything bad happened, no one had any idea as to how it happened or what caused it.  Locke believed it was impossible for anyone to know the mind of another.  It was an irrational belief that some people had supernatural powers.  He believed in empirical science, and wanted to understand the natural world.  He was also skeptical about religious faith.  He saw religion as a way of deceiving people about the nature of reality.  One of his favorite philosophical ideas was the idea of a 'tabula rasa', meaning a blank sheet of paper.  In this thought he saw ourselves as being like a slate after having been wiped clean by a supernatural force.  It was a radical idea, in that his skepticism was almost as strong as his faith, but others saw it differently.  In the modern era of science, the idea of a blank slate is replaced by the idea that every human is 'born with a blank slate', and his slate has been filled in by experiences.
